questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'What is Federalism' refers to.
questions.a: Federalism is a system of government in which power is divided between a central authority and its constituent units (states/provinces). In a federal system, the central government and state governments are both answerable to the people, and each has its own jurisdiction defined by the constitution.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'What is Federalism'.
questions.a: Federalism divides power between the central government and constituent units, with each level having its own sphere of authority guaranteed by the constitution.

questions.q: Under which section is 'What is Federalism' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: What is Federalism

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Features of Federalism' refers to.
questions.a: Federalism has key features: (1) different tiers of government with their own jurisdiction; (2) a written constitution specifying the powers of each tier; (3) each tier having its own source of revenue; and (4) the fundamental provisions of the constitution requiring consent of both levels for change. There are two routes to forming federations: coming together (independent states uniting) and holding together (a large country dividing into constituent units).

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Features of Federalism'.
questions.a: Federalism is characterised by multiple tiers with defined jurisdiction, a written constitution, independent revenue sources, and mutual consent for constitutional change.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Features of Federalism' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: Features of Federalism

concepts.title: Unitary vs Federal System of Government

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Unitary vs Federal System of Government' refers to.
questions.a: In a unitary system, the central government can pass orders to provincial governments, which are subordinate. In a federal system, the central government cannot order the state governments to do something; state governments have their own powers and are not subordinate to the centre. However, many federations have unitary features for flexibility.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Unitary vs Federal System of Government'.
questions.a: The key distinction is that in federalism, state governments are not subordinate to the central government and have their own constitutional powers, unlike in a unitary system.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Unitary vs Federal System of Government' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: Features of Federalism

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Federalism in India' refers to.
questions.a: India is a federal country with three tiers of government: the Union Government (central), State Governments, and (after 1992) local self-governments. The Constitution divides powers through the Union List, State List, and Concurrent List. India is a 'holding together' federation where the central government tends to be more powerful than the states.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Federalism in India'.
questions.a: India is a federal country with three tiers, a constitution-based division of powers, and a stronger central government typical of holding-together federations.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Federalism in India' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: Federalism in India

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Three Tiers of Government' refers to.
questions.a: Originally, India had two tiers: the Union Government and State Governments. After the 1992 constitutional amendments, a third tier of federalism - local self-government (Panchayats and Municipalities) - was added, making India a three-tier federal system.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Three Tiers of Government'.
questions.a: India's federalism has three tiers: the Union Government, State Governments, and local self-governments, the third tier added by constitutional amendment in 1992.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Three Tiers of Government' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: Federalism in India

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Linguistic States and Language Policy' refers to.
questions.a: The creation of linguistic states was the first major test of democratic politics in India. From 1947, many old states vanished and new ones were created to ensure people speaking the same language lived in the same state. India's language policy did not give the status of 'national language' to any one language; Hindi was identified as the official language, and English was retained as an associate official language. Besides, states could have their own official languages.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Linguistic States and Language Policy'.
questions.a: India accommodated linguistic diversity by creating linguistic states and adopting a flexible language policy with Hindi as official language, English as associate, and state-level official languages.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Linguistic States and Language Policy' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: Federalism in India

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Centre-State Relations and Decentralisation' refers to.
questions.a: Centre-state relations determine how federalism works in practice. Originally, the central government often misused the Constitution to dismiss state governments. After 1990, the rise of regional parties and coalition governments at the centre changed this, making the centre more respectful of state autonomy. Decentralisation is the sharing of power among nations, states, and local levels, and in India it was strengthened by the 1992 amendments that gave constitutional status to Panchayats and Municipalities.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Centre-State Relations and Decentralisation'.
questions.a: Federalism in India improved after 1990 due to coalition politics, and decentralisation was strengthened by giving constitutional status to local governments.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Centre-State Relations and Decentralisation' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: Federalism in India

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Decentralisation in India - Local Self-Government' refers to.
questions.a: Decentralisation in India involves a third tier of government - local self-government - comprising Panchayats in rural areas and Municipalities in urban areas. The 1992 constitutional amendments (73rd and 74th) gave them constitutional status, with regular elections, reservation of seats for women and marginalised groups, and devolution of powers and resources. Some states also have structures for very large states, but generally the basic structure is uniform.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Decentralisation in India - Local Self-Government'.
questions.a: Decentralisation in India created a third tier of local self-government with constitutional guarantees for elections, representation, and devolution of powers.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Decentralisation in India - Local Self-Government' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: Decentralisation in India
